# Button Mash — full context

# Button Mash

The universal in-browser game console. Three centerpieces: (1) the Player — a bring-your-own-file EmulatorJS console for 20+ classic systems (the site hosts zero ROMs; the user's file never leaves their machine); (2) the Converter — drop in a GBA, GB/GBC or NES file you own, get back a single self-contained playable .html browser game (client-side only, all three cores BIOS-free); (3) the Party Planner — headcount + time + vibe in, timed game-night rotation plan out. Plus a curated directory of 114 free, legal browser games (every link verified live 2026-10-11), hand-built collections, genre deep dives, and legal-lane emulation guides. No ROM piracy links, no cracked-game sites, no commercial ROM downloads — ever.

## Play
- player.html — the bring-your-own-file Player (EmulatorJS, 20+ systems, save states, fullscreen)
- converter.html — ROM-to-browser-game converter (GBA/GB/GBC/NES in, self-contained .html out)
- party-planner.html — timed game-night rotation planner across party-tagged games (print-friendly)
- games.html — the 114-game directory (search, genre filters, favorites, random game, game of the day)
- collections.html — 11 hand-built collections
- genres/roguelike.html, genres/cozy.html — genre deep dives with start-here picks

## Learn
- emulation.html — emulation hub
- monster-taming.html — original-IP monster-taming games + GBA-to-WASM tech
- play-legal.html — the one clear legal page

## Emulators (10 picks, software only)

- EmulatorJS [NES, SNES, GB, GBC, GBA, Genesis, Master System, Game Gear, N64, NDS, PlayStation, Atari, and more] — The engine behind this site's Player. 20+ systems in a web page; embed on any site. https://emulatorjs.org/
- RetroArch [Dozens via cores] — All-in-one frontend: install once, add one core per system. Shaders, netplay, run-ahead latency reduction, RetroAchievements. https://www.retroarch.com/
- mGBA [GBA, GB, GBC] — The accuracy king for GBA; also the core in this site's Player and Converter. No BIOS needed. https://mgba.io/
- SameBoy [GB, GBC] — Cycle-accurate Game Boy / Color emulation, beautifully maintained. https://sameboy.github.io/
- Mesen [NES, SNES, GB, GBC] — The most accurate NES emulator ever made, with a legendary debugger. Also covers SNES/GB. https://mesen.ca/
- DuckStation [PlayStation] (needs your own dumped BIOS) — Modern, fast PlayStation emulator with gorgeous upscaling. https://www.duckstation.org/
- PCSX2 [PlayStation 2] (needs your own dumped BIOS) — The long-reigning PS2 emulator, still actively improved. https://pcsx2.net/
- PPSSPP [PSP] — Plays the PSP library at HD resolutions on almost anything. https://www.ppsspp.org/
- Dolphin [GameCube, Wii] — GameCube and Wii emulation at HD resolutions. One of the most polished emulators ever made. https://dolphin-emu.org/
- webretro [Many via libretro cores] — RetroArch cores in the browser via a clean web frontend. Good alternative embedding option. https://github.com/BinBashBanana/webretro

# Guides (full text)

## EmulatorJS self-hosting guide
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~30 min · slug: emulatorjs-self-hosting

Host the open-source EmulatorJS player on your own site and play ROMs you dumped yourself — setup, cores, BIOS, and the legal line.

### What it is (and the legal line)

EmulatorJS is a free, open-source project that puts classic console emulation in a web page. It bundles libretro cores compiled to WebAssembly, so systems from the NES to the GBA run right in the browser with no plugins.

The software itself is completely legal — and it ships with zero games. You supply the game files, and this is the part that matters: only load ROMs you dumped from cartridges or discs you own, plus homebrew and public-domain titles. Downloading commercial ROMs you don't own is piracy, no matter how nicely the player is skinned.

### What you need

- A web host that serves static files (any static host works), or just your own computer for local play
- ROM files you dumped yourself — see the rip-your-own-cartridges guide
- For some systems, a BIOS file dumped from hardware you own (GBA and PlayStation cores need one)
- About 30 minutes

### 1. Get the release

Grab the latest release ZIP from the project's GitHub releases page (github.com/EmulatorJS/EmulatorJS) and unzip it into your site folder. The ZIP contains the loader, the cores, and a data directory — no installer, no build step.

If you'd rather not self-host, the project's own demo page shows the same setup; the steps below work identically on any static host.

### 2. Add your own games

Create a folder (call it `roms`) and copy in only ROMs you dumped from games you own, plus homebrew or public-domain ROMs. One subfolder per system keeps cores straight — `roms/gba/`, `roms/snes/`, and so on.

Name files clearly. EmulatorJS doesn't care about fancy naming schemes; it cares that the file is a valid dump.

### 3. Embed the player

Drop this into an HTML page where you want the game to appear:

<div id="game"></div>
<script>
  EJS_player = '#game';
  EJS_core = 'gba';                 // the core for your system
  EJS_gameUrl = 'roms/gba/mygame.gba'; // a ROM you dumped yourself
  EJS_pathtodata = 'data/';          // EmulatorJS data directory
</script>
<script src="data/loader.js"></script>

Swap `EJS_core` for the system you're playing (`snes`, `nes`, `gb`, `gba`, `n64`, `nds`, and more are supported). The full core list is in the project's documentation.

### 4. BIOS files (dump your own)

Some cores refuse to boot without a system BIOS. Dump the BIOS from hardware you own — the same dumpers in the rip-your-own guide usually handle this — and place it where the core's documentation says to look. Never download a BIOS file; like ROMs, they're copyrighted software.

### 5. Extras worth knowing

- Gamepad support is built in; most USB and Bluetooth controllers just work
- Save states live in the browser; export them if you switch devices
- Netplay is available for some cores if you want online multiplayer
- On mobile, add the page to your home screen for a near-native feel

### The rule, one more time

EmulatorJS gives you the player, not the games. If a setup tutorial tells you to download a ROM pack, close the tab — that tutorial is pointing you at piracy. Your library should be: dumps of games you physically own, homebrew from its authors, and public-domain releases. That's the whole legal lane, and it's plenty.

## RetroArch setup guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~20 min · slug: retroarch-setup

Install RetroArch, add cores for hardware you own, and load your own dumped games — controllers, save states, shaders, and netplay included.

### What it is (and the legal line)

RetroArch is a free, open-source frontend for emulators. Instead of one emulator per system, you install RetroArch once and add small emulator modules called cores — one for each console you want to play. It runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and even in a browser.

RetroArch contains no games and no BIOS files. You bring those: dumps of games you own (see the rip-your-own guide) and homebrew or public-domain titles.

### 1. Install RetroArch

Download RetroArch from retroarch.com — pick your platform. It's also on Steam and most package managers, which handle updates for you. Install it like any normal app; the first launch walks you through the basics.

### 2. Download cores (the emulators)

Go to Main Menu → Online Updater → Core Downloader. You'll see a list of cores, each named for the hardware it emulates. Install the core matching hardware you own — for example, a Game Boy Advance core if you have GBA cartridges to dump.

Cores are emulator software, and they're legal. Installing ten cores you never use harms nothing; loading a game you don't own into one is the part that's piracy.

### 3. Load your own games

Main Menu → Load Content → browse to your dumped ROM file. RetroArch will ask which core to use; pick the one you installed. To build a pretty library view, use Import Content → Scan Directory on a folder of your dumps — RetroArch matches them against its database and builds per-system playlists with box art.

### 4. Controllers

Settings → Input. Most USB and Bluetooth gamepads are recognized automatically with sane default mappings — plug in and play. If a button feels wrong, remap it per-core under Quick Menu → Controls while a game is running; RetroArch saves the remap for that core.

### 5. The good stuff: saves, shaders, netplay

- Save states: Quick Menu → Save State, with slots per game
- Rewind: enable it in Settings → Frame Throttle, then hold the rewind hotkey to scrub mistakes away
- Shaders: Quick Menu → Shaders adds CRT scanlines and other retro looks
- Netplay: Netplay menu for online multiplayer on supported cores
- Achievements: sign up at retroachievements.org and link it in Settings for retro achievements

### The rule, one more time

Keep your library to three sources: dumps of games you own, homebrew from its authors, and public-domain releases. RetroArch never asks where your files came from — that's your responsibility, and it's the whole difference between a legal retro setup and a piracy box.

## GBA-to-WASM recompiler guide
Difficulty: Advanced · ~90 min · slug: gba-to-wasm-recompiler

Turn a GBA cartridge you own into a self-contained browser page via static recompilation — the user-supplied-ROMs-only pattern, end to end.

### The pattern

Most browser emulation interprets a console's CPU in real time. A static recompiler takes a different path: it translates the game's ARM/Thumb machine code into WebAssembly ahead of time, once. The result is a self-contained web page — WASM plus a small runtime shim — that plays the game with no emulator needed at runtime.

The open-source demo at agnt-gg/gba-pokemon-rom-to-wasm walks the whole pattern end to end and is the best reference for how the pieces fit.

### The non-negotiable input rule

The input ROM must be a dump of a cartridge you physically own — see the rip-your-own-cartridges guide. Two hard rules:

1. Never feed a downloaded ROM into the toolchain. The recompiler doesn't care where the file came from; the law does.
2. Don't redistribute the built page. The output still contains the original game's copyrighted code, so sharing the build is sharing the game.

Build for yourself, play it yourself. That's the legal lane.

### 1. Dump your own cartridge

Use a cartridge dumper — a GB Operator, Joey Jr., Sanni Cart Reader, or similar — to read your own GBA cartridge into a ROM file on your computer. Verify the dump (most dumper software shows a checksum) before you build.

### 2. Run the recompiler on your dump

Clone the recompiler repository and follow its README for the toolchain install. Point the build script at your dumped ROM file. The build emits three things: a WASM module with your game's translated code, the JavaScript glue and runtime shim (this implements the GBA's graphics, sound, and timer hardware), and an HTML shell that loads it all.

### 3. Host the build yourself

The output is static files, so any static web host works — or just open the HTML file locally. Saves typically persist via localStorage or IndexedDB in the browser. Keep the page private, or share it only with people who own the same cartridge.

### How it works, briefly

At build time, each ARM instruction in the game maps to equivalent WebAssembly operations. Anything the game expects from real GBA hardware — the picture processing unit, the sound channels, the timers, the memory-mapped I/O — is implemented in the runtime shim the recompiler ships with. It's emulation, just done ahead of time instead of on the fly.

### Limits and gotchas

- Not every game recompiles cleanly; anti-piracy checks and unusual hardware tricks can break the build
- Performance varies by browser and device; desktop Chrome/Firefox are the smoothest targets
- Debugging a broken build means reading the recompiler's logs, not the game's code — start with a simple, well-documented game
- This pattern generalizes: the same idea applies to other consoles, with different recompiler projects

## Rip-your-own-cartridges guide
Difficulty: Beginner · ~45 min · slug: rip-your-own-cartridges

Turn cartridges you own into verified ROM backups with a USB dumper — hardware picks, the dumping ritual, and the no-distribution rule.

### The idea

Dumping is reading the data off a cartridge or disc you own into a file on your computer. That file — the ROM or disc image — is a backup of your property, and it's the only legal way to get game files for the emulators and recompilers in the other guides.

This guide is practical how-to, not legal advice. The general principle is simple: back up what you own, and never distribute the copies.

### The legal framing (general principles)

Making a personal backup of software you own is treated very differently from downloading or sharing copies you have no rights to. The bright line is distribution: uploading your dumps, sharing them with friends, or downloading someone else's is piracy regardless of whether you own the game.

Laws vary by country and change over time. When in doubt, the conservative read — your dumps, your devices, no sharing — keeps you safe everywhere.

### Pick a dumper for your system

- Game Boy / Game Boy Color / Game Boy Advance: GB Operator (Epilogue) or Joey Jr. — dead simple USB dumpers
- SNES + Genesis: Retrode 2 — plug the cart into a USB adapter that mounts like a drive
- Multi-system DIY: INLretro Dumper or the open-source Sanni Cart Reader — more systems, more tinkering
- Save files: most of these dumpers also back up the save RAM, so your 100-hour file survives

### The dumping ritual

1. Clean the cartridge's edge connector with isopropyl alcohol and a cotton swab — dirty contacts cause bad dumps
2. Seat the cart firmly in the dumper
3. Run the dumper software and save the ROM file
4. Verify it: good dumper software shows a checksum. Compare it against a known-good database entry for your exact cartridge — a match means a perfect read
5. Keep the physical cartridge. It's your proof of ownership and the reason the backup is yours to make

### Disc-based games

Optical media needs a compatible disc drive plus dumping software; the per-system guides in preservation communities document exact drive models and settings. The same rule applies: your disc, your dump, no sharing. Disc dumps are big — budget storage accordingly.

### Store it right

- Keep each ROM next to a small text file with its checksum and the cartridge it came from
- Back up save files separately; they're tiny and irreplaceable
- Store everything twice (local drive + a backup) — dumped once, kept forever
- Label homebrew and public-domain ROMs as such so your future self knows what's shareable

## Homebrew & public-domain sources
Difficulty: Reference · ~10 min · slug: homebrew-and-public-domain

Where to find legal homebrew ROMs and public-domain games: archives, dev communities, itch.io, and open-source originals.

### What counts as legal

Homebrew means new games made by hobbyists for old (and new) hardware, released free by their authors. Public domain means the copyright expired or was explicitly waived. Both are fully legal to download, play, and share — they're the guilt-free way to fill an emulator library or a recompiler project.

### Where to find them

- pdroms.de — a long-running archive of homebrew ROMs across dozens of systems. Everything there is distributed by its authors.
- nesdev.com — the NES homebrew development community: forums, tutorials, and released homebrew games.
- gbdev.io — the Game Boy homebrew hub: dev resources plus finished, free games.
- itch.io (itch.io/games, search 'homebrew') — many homebrew devs release ROMs free on their itch pages; filter by 'play in browser' for instant play.
- Internet Archive collections — the MS-DOS Games, Internet Arcade, and Console Living Room collections (all in our game directory) include homebrew and public-domain titles; check each item's rights statement.

### Open-source originals (not ROMs at all)

- OpenTTD (openttd.org) — a complete, open-source transport sim and a genuinely great game
- The open-source web games in our directory — 2048, Hextris, A Dark Room, and friends are free software you can also self-host
- Engine recreations exist for some classics, but they typically need original game data from a copy you own — the engine is free, the assets aren't

### The smell test

If a 'homebrew' site also offers commercial ROM downloads, leave. The test is simple: does the site point you at the game's author, or at a download button for a game Nintendo still sells? Link the guide and the tool, never the pirated content. When in doubt, the author's own page wins.

## How GBA becomes WebAssembly
Difficulty: Intermediate · ~12 min · slug: gba-wasm

The reverse-engineering pattern behind browser GBA: ARM/THUMB basic blocks lifted into real WASM, frame timing, memory mapping — original explainer.

### The CPU problem: ARM in a browser

The GBA runs on an ARM7TDMI with ARM and THUMB instruction sets. Recompilers translate the game's machine code into WebAssembly ahead of time, so the browser runs it natively instead of interpreting it.

### Basic blocks: the unit of translation

Straight-line runs of instructions become individual WASM functions; ARM registers become WASM locals; branches become a dispatch loop. Self-modifying code is handled by checksumming and retranslating.

### Memory mapping: faking the hardware

A flat WASM memory block gets a memory map on top: hardware addresses route to implementations of the PPU, sound channels, DMA, and timers. BIOS calls are reimplemented clean-room (HLE).

### Frame timing

The GBA runs at exactly 59.73 fps; the runtime paces translated code against the display and audio clocks so games run at true speed.

### Differential verification

Serious projects run the WASM translation and a trusted interpreter side by side and compare CPU state after every block — any divergence is a translation bug.

## How emulation works
Difficulty: Beginner · ~8 min · slug: how-emulation-works

Plain-English explainer: interpreters vs. recompilers, cycle accuracy, what a BIOS does, save states, and why the browser is enough now.

### The core idea

An emulator pretends to be the original chips — CPU, graphics, sound, timers — well enough that the game can't tell the difference.

### Interpreters vs. recompilers

Interpreters simulate one instruction at a time (simple, slower); recompilers translate chunks to native code ahead of time (complex, faster).

### Cycle accuracy

Old games race the hardware beam; cycle-accurate emulators simulate chips in lockstep so timing tricks work.

### What a BIOS does

Some consoles need firmware dumped from your own hardware; others (GBA via mGBA) reimplement it clean-room; some need none.

### Save states

Complete snapshots of the emulated machine — save mid-jump. In browsers they persist via local storage / IndexedDB.

## Best emulator per system
Difficulty: Reference · ~6 min · slug: best-emulator-per-system

One honest emulator pick per classic system: accuracy, ease of use, platform notes. Software only — no ROM links.

### The picks

mGBA (GBA), SameBoy (GB/GBC), Mesen (NES), Snes9x (SNES), Genesis Plus GX (Genesis), Mupen64Plus-Next (N64), DuckStation (PSX, needs your BIOS), PCSX2 (PS2, needs your BIOS), PPSSPP (PSP), melonDS (NDS), RetroArch (everything), EmulatorJS (in-browser).

### How to choose

Play in a tab: this site's Player. One system: the standalone pick. Many systems: RetroArch. Accuracy above all: Mesen, SameBoy, mGBA.
